subject: geography
prompt: Why is water described as a **renewable resource**?

image.alt: Labelled water cycle with evaporation, condensation, precipitation, run-off and groundwater

options.text: Three-fourths of the Earth is covered with water, so it can never be used up
It keeps moving through the hydrological cycle, so surface run-off and groundwater are renewed and recharged
Most of the water on Earth is already fresh enough to drink
Rain falls equally over every region in every year

hint: Think of the cycle of evaporation, clouds, rain and run-off.
explanation: All water moves within the **hydrological cycle**, and freshwater from surface run-off and groundwater is continually renewed and recharged. That is what makes it renewable. The other options fail: water covers most of the Earth but only a small part is usable freshwater, and rainfall varies greatly over space and time.

subject: geography
prompt: About what fraction of the Earth's surface is covered with water?

image.alt: Pie diagram of the Earth's surface showing water and land

options.text: One-fourth
One-half
Three-fourths
Nine-tenths

hint: Water covers far more of the surface than land does.
explanation: Roughly **three-fourths** of the Earth's surface is water. Only a small proportion of this is freshwater that can be put to use, which is why scarcity is still possible.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the place where water vapour cools and turns into tiny drops to form **clouds**.

image.alt: Water cycle: sun heats the sea, vapour rises to form clouds, rain falls on land, runs off into rivers and soaks into groundwater

hint: Condensation happens high in the sky.
explanation: Water vapour rising from the sea cools and **condenses** into droplets that form clouds. The sea is where evaporation starts, the river carries run-off, and groundwater is stored under the soil.

subject: geography
prompt: Rain that is not absorbed flows over the land. Tap the part of the picture that carries this **surface run-off** towards the sea.

image.alt: Water cycle: sun heats the sea, vapour rises to form clouds, rain falls on land, runs off into rivers and soaks into groundwater

hint: It is a stream on the land surface, not under it.
explanation: **Surface run-off** is rainwater that flows over the land into streams and rivers, and finally reaches the sea. Groundwater is the part that soaks into the soil and stays underground.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these are sources from which **freshwater** is obtained, according to the chapter?

image.alt: Water cycle: sun heats the sea, vapour rises to form clouds, rain falls on land, runs off into rivers and soaks into groundwater

options.text: Salt water of the sea
Precipitation
Groundwater
Surface run-off

hint: Freshwater comes from three parts of the hydrological cycle.
explanation: Freshwater is obtained directly from **precipitation**, **surface run-off** and **groundwater**. Sea water is salty and is not counted as a freshwater source.

subject: geography
prompt: According to the chapter, water scarcity in most cases is caused by

image.alt: Women carrying earthen pots on a long walk across dry land to fetch water

options.text: low rainfall in desert regions alone
three-fourths of the Earth being covered with water
the hydrological cycle stopping for some months
over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups

hint: Rainfall variation is only part of the story.
explanation: Water availability does vary with seasonal and annual rainfall, but scarcity in most cases comes from **over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access** among social groups. Believing that only low rainfall causes scarcity is the common mistake; cities with ample resources can also be short of water.

subject: geography
prompt: Which **two** regions are likely to suffer from water scarcity?

image.alt: Four regions compared by rainfall, population and water quality

options.text: A: Region with high annual rainfall
B: High annual rainfall and a large population
C: High annual rainfall but highly polluted water
D: Moderate rainfall, a small population and clean water

hint: Think about demand from people and about quality, not rainfall alone.
explanation: A large, growing population raises demand (for homes and for food production), and polluted water cannot be used even if there is plenty of it. So **B and C** suffer scarcity. Region A has high rainfall without these pressures, and region D has enough clean water for its few people, so neither is described as water-scarce.

subject: geography
prompt: Which activity is the **largest consumer** of water?

image.alt: A factory and a city both drawing heavily on the same freshwater

options.text: Irrigated agriculture

image.alt: A farm field being irrigated by a sprinkler

options.text: Factories

image.alt: A factory with smoking chimneys

options.text: Household use

image.alt: A house with a tap

options.text: Office and city buildings

image.alt: Tall buildings of a city

hint: Think of how much water growing food needs.
explanation: **Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water.** A large population needs water for domestic use and, above all, to produce more food, so irrigation has expanded and water resources are over-exploited.

subject: geography
prompt: Many farmers dig their own wells and tube-wells to increase their produce. Which picture shows the likely result for groundwater?

image.alt: Many tube-wells pumping groundwater for irrigation on farms

options.text: The underground water level goes up

image.alt: Underground water level higher, with an upward arrow

options.text: The underground water level stays the same

image.alt: Underground water level unchanged

options.text: The underground water level goes down

image.alt: Underground water level lower, with a downward arrow

options.text: Groundwater rises and floods the land

image.alt: Groundwater reaching the surface and flooding the land

hint: More water is pulled out than rain puts back.
explanation: Over-pumping through wells and tube-wells leads to **falling groundwater levels**, which harms water availability and food security. The other pictures show the opposite or an unchanged level.

subject: geography
prompt: Industrial growth puts great pressure on freshwater mainly because industries

image.alt: A factory and a city both drawing heavily on the same freshwater

options.text: are heavy users of water and also need power, much of which comes from hydroelectric projects
return all the water they use to rivers in clean form
are always built where rainfall is highest
reduce the demand for electricity

hint: Two demands: the factory itself and the power that runs it.
explanation: Industries are **heavy users of water** and also need **power**, and much of that energy is hydroelectric. Growing urban centres add further demand. The other options are not supported by the chapter.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A factory and a city both drawing heavily on the same freshwater

assertion: Some cities that have ample water resources still face water scarcity.
reason: Their large and growing populations raise demand and access to water is unequal.
hint: Look at the chapter's explanation of scarcity in cities.
explanation: Both statements are true and R explains A. Water scarcity may be an outcome of a **large and growing population** and the consequent greater demand, along with **unequal access**. Housing colonies drilling their own pumps over-exploit groundwater, depleting it.

subject: geography
prompt: A river is full of water but farm runoff makes it unsafe. Tap the source that adds **fertilisers and pesticides** to the river.

image.alt: A river receiving waste from a factory pipe, a house drain and runoff from a farm field

hint: Look for the cultivated land.
explanation: Fertilisers and pesticides used in **agriculture** run off from fields into the water. The factory adds industrial waste and the house drain adds domestic waste; together they pollute water that is otherwise plentiful.

subject: geography
prompt: A river has plenty of water, but villagers cannot use it because factories and farms have polluted it with chemicals. What kind of problem is this?

image.alt: A river receiving waste from a factory pipe, a house drain and runoff from a farm field

options.text: Scarcity caused only by low rainfall
Scarcity caused by bad quality of water even though the quantity is enough
A water surplus, since plenty of water is available
Scarcity caused by sedimentation in a reservoir

hint: The chapter has a second kind of scarcity besides shortage in quantity.
explanation: The chapter notes that water may be sufficient yet the area still suffers from scarcity because much of it is **polluted** by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers, making it hazardous for human use.

subject: geography
prompt: Under the Jal Jeevan Mission, piped water is to be supplied at **55 litres per capita per day**. How many litres should a rural family of **5** receive in **7 days**?

image.alt: A rural house with a tap and five family members; piped water is supplied at 55 litres per person per day

options.text: 385 litres
275 litres
67 litres
1,925 litres

hint: Multiply by persons and by days.
explanation: Per person per day is 55 L, so the family needs $55 \times 5 \times 7 = 1{,}925$ L. Traps: forgetting the 5 persons gives 385 L; forgetting the 7 days gives 275 L; adding the numbers gives 67.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these are reasons the chapter gives for conserving and managing water resources?

image.alt: Four picture cards showing things that depend on water

options.text: To safeguard ourselves from health hazards
To ensure food security and livelihoods
To prevent degradation of natural ecosystems
To encourage more dry-season irrigation with wells

hint: Over-exploitation and mismanagement impoverish the resource.
explanation: The chapter says we must conserve water to avoid **health hazards**, ensure **food security**, continue **livelihoods and productive activities** and prevent **degradation of ecosystems**. Expanding dry-season irrigation with wells is a cause of over-exploitation, not a reason to conserve.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange these developments in **time order**, earliest first.

image.alt: A time arrow with four water structures: a flood-water channel, a dam, a large lake and a masonry tank

items.text: The Hauz Khas tank in Delhi was built (13th-14th century)
Sringaverapura's system channelled flood water of the Ganga (1st century B.C.)
Multi-purpose river projects were launched after Independence
Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built (11th century)

hint: Use the centuries given in the chapter.
explanation: The order is the **1st century B.C.** channels at Sringaverapura, the **11th century** Bhopal Lake, the **13th-14th century** Hauz Khas tank, and finally the modern multi-purpose projects begun after Independence.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each structure or place with what the chapter says about it.

image.alt: Four traditional water structures: stone rubble dam, reservoir, embankment and canal

right.text: One of the largest artificial lakes of its time
Built to supply water to the Siri Fort area
Dams, lakes and irrigation systems built extensively
Water harvesting system channelling flood water of the Ganga

hint: Each is a separate bullet in the box on ancient India.
explanation: These are the examples listed under hydraulic structures in ancient India.

subject: geography
prompt: What is a **dam**?

image.alt: Cross-section of a dam: reservoir, wall, spillway gates, power house, canal and river below

options.text: A barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir
A canal that carries river water to fields
A pit dug to reach underground water
A pipe that carries rain from a roof to a tank

hint: Look at the picture: a wall across the river.
explanation: A **dam** is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir. A canal, a well and a roof pipe are different structures.

subject: geography
prompt: Timber dams, embankment dams and masonry dams are classified on the basis of

image.alt: Three dams drawn in section: made of timber, of earth and of stone masonry

options.text: their height
the purpose for which they are built
the structure and the materials used
the river basin where they stand

hint: Think about what the three names have in common: timber, earth, masonry.
explanation: Based on **structure and materials**, dams are timber, embankment or masonry. Height is a separate classification (low, medium height, high, or large and major dams), and purpose is another.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **spillway**, the part through which water is meant to flow over the dam.

image.alt: Cross-section of a dam: reservoir, wall, spillway gates, power house, canal and river below

hint: It is at the top of the dam wall.
explanation: The **spillway** or weir is the section over or through which water is intended to flow, intermittently or continuously. The reservoir stores the water, the wall holds it back and the power house produces electricity.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the part where the impounded water is used to produce **hydel power**.

image.alt: Cross-section of a dam: reservoir, wall, spillway gates, power house, canal and river below

hint: A turbine spins inside.
explanation: Water from the reservoir passes through pipes to the **power house**, whose turbine generates hydel power. The canal takes water to fields, which is the irrigation use of the same project.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these are uses for which dams are built today?

image.alt: Cross-section of a dam: reservoir, wall, spillway gates, power house, canal and river below

options.text: Electricity generation
Flood control
Supplying water for domestic and industrial use
Increasing siltation in rivers
Stopping all rainfall

hint: Modern dams are called multi-purpose projects.
explanation: Dams are built for irrigation, **electricity generation**, **water supply** for homes and industry, **flood control**, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding, so the many uses are integrated. Siltation is a side effect, not a purpose.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each project or place with what the chapter says about it.

image.alt: Three rivers each with a dam, serving power and irrigation, flood protection, or farm fields

right.text: Conserves water together with flood control (Mahanadi basin)
Built over the Narmada River in Gujarat
Diversion by Maharashtra led to a Krishna-Godavari dispute
Water used for both hydel power and irrigation (Sutlej-Beas basin)

hint: Two are examples of integration; two are about location and a dispute.
explanation: Bhakra-Nangal integrates power and irrigation; Hirakud integrates conservation with flood control; Sardar Sarovar is on the Narmada; the diversion at Koyna caused a dispute downstream.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A dam wall blocks fish swimming upstream to their spawning area

assertion: Large dams make life difficult for the aquatic animals of a river.
reason: Dams are built to generate electricity.
hint: Check each statement on its own, then ask whether R explains A.
explanation: A is true: dams **fragment rivers**, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially to spawn. R is also true (hydel power is a use of dams) but it does **not** explain the harm to river life.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these are criticisms of large dams and multi-purpose projects given in the chapter?

image.alt: Trees and soil on a flood plain lying under reservoir water, with bubbles rising as they decompose

options.text: Excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir
Existing vegetation and soil on flood plains are submerged and decompose
Fish and other aquatic animals find it hard to migrate
More silt reaches the flood plains and fertilises them

hint: Damming holds back silt.
explanation: Dams cause poor sediment flow with excessive **sedimentation** in the reservoir, **submerge vegetation and soil**, and **fragment rivers**. The fourth option is reversed: flood plains are *deprived* of silt.

subject: geography
prompt: Why does damming a river lead to land degradation on its flood plains?

image.alt: Two flood plains: one beside a free-flowing river, the other beside a river with a dam

options.text: Extra silt from the dam buries the crops under mud
Silt, a natural fertiliser, is trapped in the reservoir, so the flood plains are deprived of it
The reservoir removes salt from the soil
A stronger river flow washes the soil away

hint: Compare the soil layer in the two pictures.
explanation: Sedimentation means the flood plains are **deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser**, which adds to land degradation. The problem is too *little* silt on the plains, not too much.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Heavy rain fills a reservoir that is full of silt; water spills over the dam and floods the houses downstream

assertion: Dams built to control floods have sometimes triggered floods.
reason: Sedimentation in the reservoir can cause floods.
hint: Think about what silt does to the reservoir.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A: the chapter says dams constructed to control floods have triggered floods **due to sedimentation in the reservoir**, and big dams have mostly been unsuccessful in controlling floods at the time of excessive rainfall.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Sediment piles up on the reservoir floor behind a dam while the river below carries little silt

assertion: Regulating and damming a river does not change its natural flow or its sediment flow.
reason: Damming causes poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir.
hint: One of the statements contradicts the other.
explanation: A is false and R is true. Regulating and damming **affects the river's natural flow**, causing poor sediment flow downstream and excessive sedimentation in the reservoir, and rockier stream beds with poorer habitats for aquatic life.

subject: geography
prompt: Irrigation has led farmers in many regions to shift to water-intensive commercial crops. Which ecological consequence does the chapter link to this?

image.alt: Two crop fields: a little irrigation for a hardy crop, and heavy irrigation of a water-intensive crop

options.text: More silt fertilising the flood plains
Faster recharge of groundwater
Growth of drought-resistant crops
Salinisation of the soil

hint: Think of what builds up on heavily irrigated land.
explanation: Changed cropping patterns toward water-intensive crops have great ecological consequences like **salinisation of the soil**. Silt, recharge and drought-resistant crops are not results the chapter links to this shift.

subject: geography
prompt: The bar chart shows the area the Sardar Sarovar project irrigates in three states (Gujarat 18.45 lakh ha, Rajasthan 2,46,000 ha, Maharashtra 37,500 ha). How many times larger is the area irrigated in **Gujarat** than in **Rajasthan**?

image.alt: Bar chart of area irrigated by the Sardar Sarovar project: Gujarat 18.45, Rajasthan 2.46 and Maharashtra 0.375 lakh hectare

options.text: 7.5 times
49.2 times
about 0.13 times
about 16 times

hint: Write both areas in hectares before dividing.
explanation: Gujarat: $18.45\text{ lakh}=1{,}845{,}000$ ha; Rajasthan: $246{,}000$ ha. So $1{,}845{,}000 \div 246{,}000 = 7.5$. Traps: dividing by Maharashtra's area gives 49.2; inverting the ratio gives about 0.13; subtracting (about 16 lakh ha) gives a difference, not 'how many times'.

subject: geography
prompt: Which picture best fits the aim **'per drop more crop'** of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana?

image.alt: A farm field being irrigated

options.text: A field flooded until water runs off

image.alt: A field flooded so that water overflows and runs away

options.text: A leaking tap wasting water

image.alt: A leaking tap with water running to waste down a drain

options.text: Drip pipes giving water drop by drop at the plant roots

image.alt: Drip pipe giving water drop by drop at the roots of plants

options.text: A hose pouring water onto a paved road

image.alt: A hose pouring water on the paved road, far from the plants

hint: The aim is to improve on-farm water use efficiency.
explanation: 'Per drop more crop' is about **water-saving technologies** that raise on-farm water-use efficiency, such as drip irrigation. Flooding, leaks and a running hose all waste water. The other aim, 'har khet ko pani', means water access for every farm.

subject: geography
prompt: An upstream state diverts a large share of a river's water for a multi-purpose project and the downstream states object. Why?

image.alt: An abstract diagram: an upstream state diverts river water to a project; two states lie downstream

options.text: The project will bring too much silt to them
Less water would flow downstream, harming their agriculture and industry
The diverted water raises their groundwater too high
Dams are banned on rivers shared by states

hint: Think about what reaches the end of the river.
explanation: In the Krishna-Godavari dispute, diversion at Koyna by Maharashtra could **reduce downstream flow** with adverse consequences for agriculture and industry in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. The other reasons are invented.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of the following is **not** an argument in favour of multi-purpose river projects?

image.alt: A balance scale weighing the benefits of multi-purpose projects against concerns about them

options.text: They bring water to areas facing scarcity
By regulating water flow they help control floods
They generate electricity for industries and homes
They lead to large-scale displacement and loss of livelihoods

hint: Three options are benefits; one is a concern.
explanation: Bringing water, controlling floods and generating power are **benefits**. Displacement and loss of livelihood count against such projects.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each traditional method with the place and use described in the chapter.

image.alt: Four traditional rainwater harvesting methods: hill channel to a tank, flood channels, a field bund and a rooftop tank
A diversion channel on a hillside leading to a round village tank
Channels carrying flood water from a river over flat farm land
A farm field with a raised earth bund holding rainwater so that it soaks the soil
A house whose roof pipe feeds an underground tank

right.text: Flood plains of Bengal: irrigating fields
Fields turned into rain-fed storage in Jaisalmer and other parts of Rajasthan
Underground tanks for drinking water in western Rajasthan
Western Himalayas: diversion channels for agriculture

hint: Match the landscape in each little picture to the region.
explanation: Each community used the technique suited to its local ecology: hill channels in the Himalayas, inundation channels in Bengal, khadins and johads in arid Rajasthan, and tankas for drinking water.

subject: geography
prompt: A household's tanka in Phalodi was 6.1 m deep, 4.27 m long and 2.44 m wide. Treating it as a rectangular box, what is its capacity?

image.alt: A box-shaped underground tank 6.1 m deep, 4.27 m long and 2.44 m wide drawn to scale

options.text: 12.81 cubic metres
26.05 cubic metres
About 63.55 cubic metres
635.5 cubic metres

hint: Capacity of a box is length times width times depth.
explanation: $6.1 \times 4.27 \times 2.44 \approx 63.55$ m$^3$. Traps: adding the three sides gives 12.81; multiplying only two sides gives 26.05 (an area); a decimal slip gives 635.5.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the stages of **rooftop rainwater harvesting** shown in the picture, from the roof to the underground.

image.alt: Rooftop rainwater harvesting: roof, pipe, filter, sump, well and groundwater

items.text: An underground pipe takes it to a sump for immediate use
Rain falls on the roof and a PVC pipe collects it
Excess water from the sump is taken to the well
The water is filtered using sand and bricks
Water from the well recharges the underground water

hint: Follow the water along the pipes in the picture.
explanation: The sequence is roof and PVC pipe, sand and brick filter, underground pipe to the sump, excess to the well, and then recharge of groundwater. Water can be taken from the well later.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the part that **filters** the collected rainwater using sand and bricks.

image.alt: Rooftop rainwater harvesting: roof, pipe, filter, sump, well and groundwater

hint: It sits just after the roof pipe.
explanation: Rooftop water is collected in a PVC pipe and then **filtered using sand and bricks**. The sump stores filtered water for immediate use and the well helps recharge groundwater.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **underground tank (sump)** that stores filtered water for immediate use.

image.alt: Rooftop rainwater harvesting: roof, pipe, filter, sump, well and groundwater

hint: An underground pipe takes the water here.
explanation: An underground pipe carries filtered water to the **sump** for immediate use; any excess goes to the well. The well, not the sump, recharges the underground water.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the underground structure where rainwater from the roof was stored in the **Thar**.

image.alt: A house in the Thar with a sloping roof, a pipe and an underground tanka beside a cool underground room

hint: It could be as large as a big room.
explanation: In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, houses had underground **tanks or tankas**, built inside the main house or courtyard and joined by a pipe to the sloping roof. Some houses also had cool rooms beside the tanka.

subject: geography
prompt: Why was the **first spell of rain** usually not collected in the tanka?

image.alt: A house in the Thar with a sloping roof, a pipe and an underground tanka beside a cool underground room

options.text: It is too heavy for the pipe to carry
Tankas can only be filled once the monsoon ends
It is stored separately in wells
It would clean the roof and the pipes, so only later showers were stored

hint: Think about what is on the roof before the rain.
explanation: The first spell of rain **cleans the roof and the pipes**, so it is let go; rainwater from the subsequent showers is collected in the tanka.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A house in the Thar with a sloping roof, a pipe and an underground tanka beside a cool underground room

assertion: In western Rajasthan, the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting is declining.
reason: The region now receives much more rainfall than before.
hint: Recall what the chapter says is now available in western Rajasthan.
explanation: A is true but R is false. The practice declines because plenty of water is available from the **perennial Indira Gandhi Canal**, not because rainfall has increased. Some houses keep their tankas since they do not like the taste of tap water, and rainwater (palar pani) is considered the purest natural water.

subject: geography
prompt: A Shillong household needs 400 litres of water a day. If rooftop harvesting meets 15-25 per cent of its need, how much comes from the roof each day?

image.alt: Stacked bar of a household's water need with the rooftop-harvesting share of 15 to 25 per cent, beside heavy rain at Cherrapunjee

options.text: 60 to 100 litres
15 to 25 litres
300 to 340 litres
6 to 10 litres

hint: Find 15% and 25% of 400.
explanation: $400 \times 0.15 = 60$ L and $400 \times 0.25 = 100$ L. Traps: reading the percentages as litres (15-25); giving the share that is *not* met (300-340); a decimal slip (6-10).

subject: geography
prompt: Which statement about **Gendathur**, a village in Mysuru, Karnataka, is correct?

image.alt: Flow of figures for rooftop harvesting at Gendathur: 1,000 mm rain, 80 per cent collected, about 10 fillings, about 50,000 litres per house

options.text: It is a city in Meghalaya built around underground tankas
About 200 households installed rooftop harvesting and the village became rich in rainwater
Its systems collect all the rain that falls, so efficiency is 100 per cent
Each house collects about 5,00,000 litres a year

hint: Use the figures in the flow chart.
explanation: With 1,000 mm of rain, **80 per cent** collection efficiency and about 10 fillings, a house collects about **50,000 litres** a year. About 200 households installed the system and the village earned the rare distinction of being rich in rainwater.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each scheme with its aim as described in the chapter.

image.alt: Three icons: a house with a tap, drip irrigation on a farm, and villagers around a water drop

right.text: Assured potable piped water to every rural household at 55 litres per capita per day
Protective irrigation for all farms: 'har khet ko pani' and 'per drop more crop'
Behavioural change from consumption to conservation in 8220 water-stressed Gram Panchayats of 80 districts

hint: Atal Jal is about community behaviour and groundwater-stressed areas.
explanation: Atal Jal covers 8220 water-stressed Gram Panchayats in 229 blocks of 80 districts in seven states; the Jal Jeevan Mission supplies tap water at 55 litres per capita per day; the PMKSY expands assured irrigation and water-saving.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each place with the fact the chapter gives about it.

image.alt: Four village and town scenes: an underground tank, a house with a rule tick, a rainy rooftop, and a village of tanks

right.text: 15-25 per cent of a household's water needs from rooftops
First state to make rooftop harvesting compulsory in all houses
Tank 6.1 m deep, 4.27 m long and 2.44 m wide

hint: Think of the number or legal fact attached to each place.
explanation: These are the specific facts of the chapter's examples: the Phalodi tank, Shillong's rooftop share, Gendathur's 200 households and Tamil Nadu's compulsory rule, which has legal provisions to punish defaulters.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the part where the bamboo pipes pass over a road, **high above the land**.

image.alt: Bamboo drip irrigation: pipes carry spring water downhill by gravity, over a road and on to the plants

hint: It rises above the grey strip.
explanation: In the bamboo drip system, if the pipes pass a road they are **taken high above the land**. Springs on the hilltop feed the channel, and the last section drops water near the plant roots.

subject: geography
prompt: Which statement describes the **bamboo drip irrigation system** of Meghalaya correctly?

image.alt: Bamboo drip irrigation: pipes carry spring water downhill by gravity, over a road and on to the plants

options.text: Pumps lift river water into bamboo pipes that spray it widely over fields
Bamboo pipes store rainwater from roofs in underground tanks
Bamboo channels carry flood water to large reservoirs
A 200-year-old system in which bamboo pipes carry spring water downhill by gravity and finally release only 20-80 drops per minute at the plant

hint: Water starts as 18-20 litres and ends as drops.
explanation: In Meghalaya, bamboo pipes divert perennial springs on hilltops to lower reaches by **gravity**; about 18-20 litres enters the system and is reduced to **20-80 drops per minute** at the plant. It does not use pumps, roofs or flood water.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the stages of the water cycle shown in the picture in order.

image.alt: Water cycle: sun heats the sea, vapour rises to form clouds, rain falls on land, runs off into rivers and soaks into groundwater

items.text: Precipitation falls on the land
The sun heats sea water and it evaporates
Run-off and infiltration refill rivers and groundwater
Water vapour condenses to form clouds

hint: Water goes up, then comes down.
explanation: The cycle runs from evaporation to condensation, precipitation and then run-off and infiltration, which renew surface water and groundwater (the process the chapter calls the hydrological cycle).

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange how a tanka works, starting with the rain.

image.alt: A house in the Thar with a sloping roof, a pipe and an underground tanka beside a cool underground room

items.text: Water from later showers flows down the pipe
Rain falls on the sloping roof
The water is stored in the underground tanka till the next rain
The first spell cleans the roof and pipes and is not collected

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the path of water in the bamboo drip system, from source to plant.

image.alt: Bamboo drip irrigation: pipes carry spring water downhill by gravity, over a road and on to the plants

items.text: Branch pipes distribute it at the plant site
Hilltop spring water is diverted into bamboo pipes
The last channel section drops water near the plant's roots
Gravity carries it downhill through the channel sections

hint: From hilltop to roots.
explanation: Perennial spring water on the hilltop is diverted into bamboo pipes, flows by gravity through channel sections, is distributed into branches, and the last section drops water near the roots.
